What happens to my X (Twitter) when I die?

By the Afterkeep research team · Reviewed on 15 Oct 2026

Short answer: X doesn't memorialise accounts and won't give anyone access, including family. An immediate family member or a person authorised to act for the estate can ask X to deactivate the account. X then asks for details of the deceased, a copy of the requester's ID and a death certificate. Download your own archive now if you want posts kept.

Key facts

  • No memorialisation
  • No account access for family
  • Deactivation on request
  • Needs: requester ID + death certificate

How do I prepare my X (Twitter) account?

  1. Download your archive now: Settings → Your account → Download an archive of your data.
  2. Note the account in your digital estate plan with your wishes.
  3. After a death, family submit X's deceased-user request with ID and a death certificate.

Read the official policy ↗

What documents do heirs need?

  • Details of the deceased and their @username
  • A copy of your government ID
  • A copy of the death certificate

How long does it take?

X emails instructions after the request is submitted; no fixed processing time is published.

What can't be recovered?

  • Direct messages
  • Posts, once the account is deactivated, unless someone downloaded an archive beforehand

Frequently asked questions

What happens to my X (Twitter) when I die?

X doesn't memorialise accounts and won't give anyone access, including family. An immediate family member or a person authorised to act for the estate can ask X to deactivate the account. X then asks for details of the deceased, a copy of the requester's ID and a death certificate. Download your own archive now if you want posts kept.

Will X give my family my DMs?

No. X won't provide account access to anyone, including family.

Can I keep a copy of my posts for family?

Yes. Request your archive in Settings → Your account → Download an archive of your data, and store it with your digital estate plan.

Who can ask X to deactivate an account?

An immediate family member or someone authorised to act on behalf of the estate.
